what-is-cyber-security.overview: Cyber security is the practice of protecting systems, networks, data and people from damage and misuse. It is not a single product you install. It is a set of decisions about what matters, what could go wrong, and how much effort each risk deserves.
how_it_works: Every asset you rely on — a laptop, a database, a payment API, an employee's account — has an owner, a value and a lifetime.
Threats are the parties and events that could cause harm: attackers, malware, accidental mistakes, hardware failure, and insiders.
Vulnerabilities are the weaknesses those threats exploit. A system with no known weakness is not a safe system; it is an unexamined one.
Controls reduce risk. Some prevent an attack, some detect it, some limit the damage after it happens.
Security work is a loop: identify what matters, test what could break, apply controls, then verify the controls still work.
history: Security existed long before computers: locks, guards, accounting and physical safes protected the same three things we now call confidentiality, integrity and availability.
As computing moved onto shared networks in the 1980s and 1990s, the problem shifted from protecting one machine to protecting many connected ones.
The internet made that harder still, because identity became hard to establish and the number of remote users grew without bound.
Organisations now publish structured guidance so that security is repeatable rather than folklore: the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the CIS Controls, and the OWASP Top 10 are widely used references.
real_world: A hospital loses record availability when a backup cannot be restored, and patients feel it as cancelled appointments rather than as a security incident.
A retailer treats payment card numbers as the assets that matter most, and invests in segmentation and monitoring to protect them.
A small charity is targeted by the same automated credential-stuffing traffic as a large bank, because attack tooling is cheap and automated.
what_to_look_for: Write down what you are protecting and who would be harmed if it were unavailable, altered, or disclosed.
Notice where trust is granted automatically, because unexamined trust is where most incidents begin.
Ask what would happen if this component failed, and whether anyone would notice within minutes or within months.
Distinguish a bug from a security issue: it only becomes security-relevant when it crosses a boundary someone was supposed to control.
defensive: Keep a written inventory of the assets that actually matter to you.
Prioritise by impact, not by how interesting a control is to implement.
Prefer boring, well-understood controls over clever ones you cannot maintain.
Test your defences deliberately, in a way that is authorised and safe.
Treat recovery as a security control: backups, tested restores and rehearsed downtime plans.

cybersecurity-vs-information-security.overview: Information security protects data wherever it lives. Cyber security is broader: it covers the technology, the networks and the services built on that data. The difference is scope, not intent.
how_it_works: Information security is about confidentiality, integrity and availability of information, regardless of the medium that holds it.
Cyber security adds the systems and supply chain: operating systems, networks, endpoints, identity providers, cloud platforms and third-party vendors.
A physical control such as a locked server room is an information-security measure expressed in a cyber environment.
Operational security covers the process side: who is allowed to change a system, how changes are approved, and how incidents are escalated.
The fields overlap heavily, and in most job descriptions the words are used interchangeably.
history: The term information security grew out of document handling and records management, long before networked computing.
As systems became interconnected, the field split into computer security, network security and information security, because each layer needed different controls.
Cyber security emerged as an umbrella term in the 1990s as attacks shifted from isolated machines to connected enterprise networks.
Today the two words are largely interchangeable in job titles, and the distinction matters mainly when scoping a policy or a compliance regime.
real_world: An ISO 27001 audit is an information-security exercise that necessarily covers the cyber systems holding that information.
A data-protection regulator focuses on personal data specifically, which is a subset of everything an organisation treats as information.
A lost company laptop is both a physical-security loss and an information-security loss, and the response depends on which data was on it.
what_to_look_for: Ask which asset class is at stake: data, a running service, a device, or a person's safety.
Check whether a control protects the information or merely the system that serves it.
Notice when a vendor promises a security product but never states which information it is meant to protect.
defensive: Write policies against the data and services you care about rather than against the tool you happen to own.
Map regulatory obligations to the specific information they cover.
Keep physical, operational and technical controls in one register so gaps between them are visible.

cia-triad.overview: The CIA triad is the standard way to describe what security protects: confidentiality, integrity and availability. Most real security work is a trade-off between these three under time and cost pressure.
how_it_works: Confidentiality limits who can read information. Encryption, access control and correct permissions are the usual controls.
Integrity means you can trust that information has not been altered without authorisation. Hashing, signatures and validation serve this goal.
Availability means authorised users can reach the information when they need it. Redundancy, capacity planning and recovery planning protect it.
Authenticity and non-repudiation are usually treated as extensions, because you cannot verify who sent a message or deny sending it without them.
A control that protects one property often weakens another, which is why security decisions are always trade-offs rather than pure gains.
history: The triad predates computing, appearing in early military and diplomatic security doctrine as confidentiality, integrity and availability.
It entered information-systems security in the 1970s and 1980s and has remained the core framing ever since.
Later work added authenticity, accountability and privacy, and some frameworks propose many more properties, but the triad remains the shared vocabulary.
Cloud platforms made the availability side more explicit, because on-demand scaling and multi-zone design are now default expectations.
real_world: A ransomware incident is usually an availability failure first, and only later a confidentiality and integrity failure once data is exfiltrated.
Enforcing multi-factor authentication on a shared administrator account improves confidentiality and may reduce availability if the second factor is unreliable.
A file-integrity monitoring tool is deployed mainly to detect integrity failures, but its logs are equally useful for accountability.
what_to_look_for: For each control you plan to add, name which of the three properties it protects and which it might weaken.
Test that availability claims are real by attempting a restore, not by confirming that a backup job reported success.
Check whether integrity protection covers configuration and code, or only user data.
defensive: Decide explicitly which properties matter most for each system and record the reason.
Protect integrity first, because undetected corruption is harder to detect than an outage.
Test restores on a schedule and record how long recovery actually takes.
Use layered controls so a failure in one layer does not remove an entire property.

assets-threats-vulnerabilities-and-risk.overview: Asset, threat, vulnerability and risk are four different ideas that get used interchangeably. Keeping them separate is what makes risk assessment possible rather than an exercise in worry.
how_it_works: An asset is anything of value that an attacker would want: data, hardware, credentials, availability, or your reputation.
A threat is a potential cause of harm, from an external attacker to an insider mistake to a hardware fault.
A vulnerability is a weakness that a threat could exploit. Not every vulnerability is exploitable, and not every exploit needs a vulnerability you knew about.
Risk is the combination of likelihood and impact. It is what you are actually trying to reduce.
Risk equals threat times vulnerability times exposure. Removing any one of the three is usually cheaper than adding another control.
history: The vocabulary comes from risk management traditions in insurance, insurance and safety engineering, and was borrowed by computing in the 1970s.
Early systems treated risk informally; formal methods such as fault trees, attack trees and the National Information Assurance Academy glossary formalised the language.
Modern practice adds likelihood scoring and business impact, so that a technical finding can be ranked against cost and effort.
The FAIR and NIST approaches differ in detail, but both insist that risk is about the business, not only about the technology.
real_world: An unpatched web server is a vulnerability; an attacker who scans for it is a threat; the combination is the risk that decides patch timing.
The same vulnerability in an isolated lab and in an internet-facing production host is a completely different risk, because exposure differs.
A medium-severity finding can outrank a critical one when it affects the only system the business can serve from.
what_to_look_for: Build the asset list before scanning, so findings are ranked by what they actually threaten.
Record exposure: reachable from the internet, reachable by staff, or reachable only by administrators.
Separate a theoretical weakness from a demonstrated exploit path before prioritising work.
Note the compensating controls that already reduce likelihood.
defensive: Maintain an asset inventory with an owner for each entry.
Rank findings by risk, not by scanner severity, and record the reason for each deferral.
Track exposure separately from vulnerability so reducing reach is visible as progress.
Revisit the assessment when the system changes, not only on a fixed calendar.

attack-surface-and-attack-vectors.overview: Attack surface is everything an attacker can reach. Attack vectors are the specific routes they use. Reducing surface is one of the most reliable ways to reduce risk.
how_it_works: Surface includes network-exposed ports, public web endpoints, mobile application code, third-party scripts, and user-facing input.
A vector is a concrete path, such as credential reuse, an unpatched dependency, a malicious attachment, or a misconfigured storage bucket.
Attackers enumerate surface automatically and continuously, so anything reachable is discovered eventually.
Reducing surface means removing reachability, not merely hiding it, because hidden interfaces are still exploitable.
Each exposed service is also an operational and patching commitment you must keep.
history: The term comes from physical security, where an attack surface is the exposed exterior of a defended building.
Software engineering adopted it in the 1990s as internet-facing services multiplied.
Cloud computing widened surface again, because storage, queues and serverless functions become reachable through credentials rather than ports.
Modern frameworks add supply-chain surface, because one compromised dependency reaches every consumer at once.
real_world: An S3 bucket left publicly readable is a single misconfiguration that exposes far more data than the application ever did.
A forgotten admin endpoint still running in production is common surface that nobody is testing any more.
A third-party analytics script on a payment page inherits the trust of the page it is embedded in.
what_to_look_for: List every externally reachable host, port, hostname and API endpoint, including test environments.
Check for default credentials, sample applications and debug modes left enabled.
Look for internal services that assume the network is trusted.
Review third-party and supply-chain dependencies, not only your own code.
defensive: Remove anything you do not need; the cheapest control is the service you never deployed.
Restrict reachability with network policy, private subnets and identity-based access.
Run internet-wide discovery continuously and alert on new exposure.
Patch and maintain every service you choose to keep reachable.

security-controls.overview: A security control is any measure that reduces risk. Controls are usually described by when they act: preventive, detective, or responsive. Effective programmes use all three.
how_it_works: Preventive controls stop an attack before it succeeds, such as authentication, authorisation, input validation and network segmentation.
Detective controls reveal that something is happening, such as logging, monitoring and file-integrity checking.
Responsive controls limit the damage and restore normal service, such as isolation, revocation and tested recovery.
Controls are also administrative, technical, or physical, and the classification matters when you assess coverage.
Compensating controls reduce risk without removing the underlying weakness, and are legitimate when the real fix is not yet available.
history: Controls existed as physical measures long before computing, and the preventive-detective-responder framing grew out of that tradition.
Compliance frameworks in the 1990s turned controls into a checkable list, which made coverage measurable but often reduced controls to paperwork.
The concept of defence in depth became central after incidents showed that any single control can fail.
Modern frameworks such as the CIS Controls emphasise prioritisation and verification rather than exhaustive control lists.
real_world: Multi-factor authentication is preventive, a login alert is detective, and a session revocation process is responsive.
A firewall rule that is never tested is documentation, not a control.
Backups only count as a control once a restore has been demonstrated, because an untested backup is an assumption.
what_to_look_for: For each control, state which risk it addresses and what happens if it fails.
Check that detective controls actually alert someone who can act on the alert.
Look for controls that exist on paper but are not enforced by tooling.
Verify that a control you rely on has been tested recently, not just deployed.
defensive: Layer controls so a single failure does not remove a whole protection.
Test detective controls by triggering them deliberately in a safe environment.
Document the failure mode of every critical control, not just its function.
Retire controls that no longer map to a current risk.

security-mindset.overview: A security mindset is the habit of asking where trust is granted, what would fail, and who benefits. It matters more than any single tool, because tools are used by people who make assumptions.
how_it_works: Assume any input can be hostile, including input from inside your network and from your own systems.
Verify decisions at the point where they matter, on the server, rather than trusting a value that crossed a boundary.
Prefer explicit denials over implicit trust, so that forgetting to add an allow rule fails safely.
Question authority, but also question your own assumptions in the opposite direction, because over-trust and under-trust both cause incidents.
Treat security as a habit of small checks rather than a project that ends at launch.
history: The idea that most incidents come from ordinary mistakes rather than genius attackers has been argued since early security research.
Formalised as a discipline in the 1990s through lessons from cryptography failures and simple configuration errors.
The term became common after high-profile breaches in which every component behaved as designed yet the system still failed.
It is now taught as a core habit, because technical controls cannot substitute for judgement at design time.
real_world: A team that reviews who can reach production before shipping ships safer code than a team that adds a scanner later.
An administrator who asks why a service needs internet access usually finds that it does not.
A developer who writes the permission check on the server, rather than relying on a hidden button, prevents a whole class of incident.
what_to_look_for: Ask where a value crossed a boundary and who vouched for it.
Notice controls that live only in the interface, since the user controls the client.
Look for defaults that fail open, such as a permission that is granted unless explicitly removed.
Check whether the failure case was designed, or whether it was never considered.
defensive: Make the secure path the easy path, so good defaults are the default.
Review trust boundaries during design rather than after a finding.
Write down what you are assuming when a system is built, and revisit those assumptions.
Reward the person who reports a weak assumption, not only the person who ships a feature.
